lessons.electrical-hazards-overview:
**Understanding Electrical Hazards in Construction**

Construction sites contain many potential electrical hazards. Workers may encounter overhead or underground power lines, damaged cords, defective tools, energized equipment, wet conditions, temporary wiring, and improperly protected circuits. Electricity is hazardous because the body can become part of an electrical circuit. A damaged cord, wet connector, missing ground prong, exposed wire, or improperly grounded tool can turn routine work into a life-threatening situation. OSHA 1926 Subpart K covers construction electrical safety requirements, including general requirements, wiring design, wiring methods, and employee protection from electrical hazards.

• Construction sites contain multiple electrical hazards, many of which are not immediately visible.
• The body can become part of an electrical circuit when contact is made with an energized source.
• Damaged insulation, missing ground prongs, and wet connectors are common hidden hazards.
• OSHA 1926 Subpart K establishes construction electrical safety requirements.
lessons.electrical-injuries:
**Electrical Injuries: Shock, Burns, Arc Flash, and Electrocution**

Electrical shock occurs when current passes through the body. Severity depends on the path of the current, the amount of current, exposure time, and whether skin is wet or dry — wet skin significantly increases shock severity. Electrical burns may be caused by arc flash, thermal contact, or current flowing through tissue and bone. Arc flash can release intense heat, light, and pressure without direct contact with an energized part. Fires may result from damaged wiring, overloaded circuits, or defective cords. Explosions can occur when electricity ignites flammable vapors, gases, or dust. Electrocution is, by definition, a fatal exposure to electrical energy and has been a leading cause of death in construction.

• Electrical shock severity depends on current path, amount, exposure time, and skin condition.
• Wet or damp skin increases the danger of electrical shock.
• Arc flash can cause severe burns and blast injuries without direct contact with energized parts.
• Electrocution is a fatal electrical event — it is distinct from non-fatal electrical shock.
lessons.major-electrocution-hazards:
**Major Electrocution Hazards on Construction Sites**

The three major categories of electrocution hazards in construction are: (1) contact with overhead or underground power lines, (2) direct contact with energized sources such as bare wires, live machine parts, defective tools, or energized metal parts, and (3) improper use of flexible cords and extension cords. Power lines may carry extremely high voltage and are hazardous whether covered or bare. Energized source contact can occur when a worker touches two wires, one energized wire and ground, or a metal part that has become energized. Flexible cords are vulnerable because they are dragged, bent, stepped on, exposed to weather, and used around rough surfaces and sharp edges.

• The three major electrocution hazard categories: power lines, energized sources, and flexible cord misuse.
• Power lines are hazardous at any voltage and whether covered or bare.
• Energized source contact includes bare wires, defective tools, and metal parts that have become live.
• Flexible cords are at high risk of damage in rough construction environments.
lessons.overhead-power-lines:
**Working Safely Around Overhead Power Lines**

Workers must always know where overhead power lines are located relative to their work. Equipment, tools, ladders, loads, materials, and workers must be kept a safe distance from energized lines. OSHA 1926.1408 requires employers to determine power line voltage, minimum approach distances, and measures to prevent encroachment. Covered lines must never be treated as safe to touch — protective coverings are weather protection, not worker insulation. Safe practices include storing materials away from beneath power lines (cranes and forklifts cannot safely retrieve materials stored under energized lines), using nonconductive ladders and tools, and coordinating with utilities to de-energize and ground lines when possible.

• Identify overhead power line locations before any work begins near them.
• Covered overhead lines are NOT safe to touch — the covering is weather protection, not insulation.
• Never store materials under overhead power lines — retrieval requires equipment that could contact the lines.
• OSHA 1926.1408 requires evaluation of power line voltage and minimum approach distances.
lessons.underground-power-lines:
**Underground Power Lines and Excavation Precautions**

Underground power lines are as dangerous as overhead lines and can be struck during digging, trenching, drilling, or other excavation activities. Before any excavation begins, the local underground utility locating service must be contacted. Workers must understand the color-coded markings, review locating documentation, and verify utility locations before beginning work. Hand digging is required within the immediate vicinity of an underground power line location. Workers must also remember that more than one cable may be buried near a single marker.

• Contact the underground utility locating service before any excavation or digging begins.
• Understand utility marking colors and verify locations before breaking ground.
• Use hand digging methods when working within the immediate vicinity of a marked utility.
• Multiple cables may be buried near a single utility marker.
lessons.gfci-protection:
**Ground-Fault Circuit Interrupters (GFCIs)**

A GFCI detects current leakage or a ground fault and interrupts the flow of electricity before it can cause severe or fatal shock. Three types are available: receptacle GFCIs installed in outlet boxes, portable or temporary GFCIs built into an extension cord or device, and circuit-breaker GFCIs installed in a panel to protect an entire circuit. Receptacle GFCIs should be tested after installation and at least monthly. Portable GFCIs should be tested before each use. If a GFCI fails its test, it must be removed from service immediately — resetting repeatedly is not acceptable. When an Assured Equipment Grounding Conductor Program is used instead of GFCIs, a written program description must be kept at the jobsite.

• A GFCI detects ground faults and interrupts electricity before a shock becomes fatal.
• Receptacle GFCIs must be tested after installation and at least monthly.
• Portable GFCIs must be tested before each use.
• A GFCI that fails its test must be removed from service immediately.
lessons.tools-extension-cords:
**Portable Power Tools and Extension Cord Safety**

Power tools and extension cords must be inspected before every use. Warning signs include damaged insulation, missing ground prongs, cracked plugs, loose connectors, exposed wires, or signs of overheating. Workers must never carry a tool by its cord, pull a cord from a receptacle by yanking the cord, run cords through water, use indoor-only equipment outdoors, or use cords not rated for hard or extra-hard use in construction conditions. Cords must be protected from heat, oil, sharp edges, moving equipment, pinch points, and trip hazards. Wrapping electrical tape around a damaged cord is not an acceptable repair. Damaged tools and cords must be removed from service immediately.

• Inspect all tools and cords before every use for damage, missing ground prongs, and signs of overheating.
• Never use indoor-only tools or cords in outdoor or damp construction conditions.
• Taping a damaged cord is not an acceptable repair — remove it from service.
• Never carry a tool by its cord or yank a cord from a receptacle.
lessons.unsafe-electrical-practices:
**Common Unsafe Electrical Practices**

Recurring unsafe practices increase the risk of electrical shock, burns, fire, and electrocution. Common violations include removing ground prongs from three-prong plugs to fit two-slot outlets, using two-prong adapters, creating makeshift extension cords from building wire, using multi-receptacle boxes as portable receptacles, using equipment in locations it is not rated for, failing to install faceplates on outlets, and using circuit breakers or fuses rated too high for the circuit. A higher-rated breaker may not trip during an overload, increasing fire and shock risk rather than providing protection. Workers must never modify cords, plugs, breakers, or other electrical protection devices.

• Never remove the ground prong from a three-prong plug — it eliminates grounding protection.
• Do not use two-prong adapters, makeshift extension cords, or indoor equipment outdoors.
• A circuit breaker rated too high for the circuit may fail to trip during an overload.
• Never modify electrical cords, plugs, breakers, or protective devices.
lessons.lockout-tagout-deenergization:
**Lockout/Tagout and De-Energizing Equipment**

Before servicing or repairing electrically powered equipment, simply turning a switch off is not sufficient protection. Proper lockout/tagout requires notifying affected workers, identifying all electrical energy sources including backup sources such as generators and batteries, turning off energy sources, applying locks and tags, testing to verify de-energization, and releasing stored energy through bleeding, blocking, grounding, or other appropriate methods. Only qualified persons may verify when it is safe to re-energize circuits or perform work on energized electrical circuits when de-energization is not possible. Overlooking a backup generator or secondary power source is a common and potentially fatal mistake.

• Turning a switch off is not sufficient — de-energize, lock out, tag out, and verify zero energy.
• Identify all energy sources including backup generators and batteries before applying lockout.
• Test to verify de-energization before beginning any service or repair work.
• Only a qualified person may determine when it is safe to re-energize electrical circuits.
